import numpy as np

im = np.array(Image.open('barcode.png').convert('RGB')).astype(float)

r,g,b = col[:,0], col[:,1], col[:,2]
lum = col.mean(axis=1)
print("mean RGB", col.mean(axis=0))
print("lum: min %.1f max %.1f mean %.1f" % (lum.min(), lum.max(), lum.mean()))

# Hue analysis
import colorsys
hues = []
for px in col:
    h,s,v = colorsys.rgb_to_hsv(px[0]/255, px[1]/255, px[2]/255)
    hues.append((h*360, s, v))
hues = np.array(hues)

# Saturation vs value quadrants
mask_dark = hues[:,2] < 0.25
mask_bright = ~mask_dark
for name, m in [("dark", mask_dark), ("bright", mask_bright)]:

    if len(sub)==0: continue
    # classify hue
    hh = sub[:,0]
    cats = {
        "red": ((hh<20)|(hh>=340)).sum(),
        "orange/yellow": ((hh>=20)&(hh<70)).sum(),
        "green": ((hh>=70)&(hh<170)).sum(),
        "cyan/blue": ((hh>=170)&(hh<260)).sum(),

        "achromatic(low sat)": (sub[:,1]<0.15).sum(),

from PIL import Image
import numpy as np

im = np.array(Image.open('barcode.png').convert('RGB')).astype(float)
col = im.mean(axis=0)

# vertical uniformity check: per-column std across rows
vstd = im.std(axis=0).mean(axis=1)
print("vertical std: mean %.2f max %.2f" % (vstd.mean(), vstd.max()))

# stripe boundaries: big jumps between adjacent columns
diff = np.abs(np.diff(col, axis=0)).sum(axis=1)
bnd = np.where(diff > 60)[0]
print("num boundaries >60:", len(bnd))
print("boundaries:", bnd.tolist())

# darkness timeline
lum = col.mean(axis=1)
darkmask = lum < 60
print("fraction dark (<60):", darkmask.mean().round(3))
# contiguous dark runs
runs=[]
i=0
while i<1000:
    if darkmask[i]:
        j=i
        while j<1000 and darkmask[j]: j+=1
        runs.append((i,j-1,j-i))
        i=j
    else: i+=1
print("dark runs (start,end,len):")
for r in runs:
    if r[2]>=5: print("  ",r)
EOF

***Manos: The Hands of Fate*** is a 1966 [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") [independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_film "Independent film") [folk horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_horror "Folk horror") film written, directed, and produced by Harold P. Warren.[\[3\]](#cite_note-AFIsearch-3) It stars Warren, Tom Neyman, John Reynolds, and Diane Mahree. It was released on November 15, 1966\. The film follows a family getting lost during their vacation road trip through the [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas") desert and becoming stranded at the lodge of a [polygynous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygyny "Polygyny") [pagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pagan "Pagan") [cult](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult "Cult") led by the Master who decides their fate.

Warren was an [insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurance "Insurance") and fertilizer salesman from [El Paso, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Paso,_Texas "El Paso, Texas"), who made the film as a result of a bet with screenwriter [Stirling Silliphant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling_Silliphant "Stirling Silliphant"). Most of the remaining cast and crew had little or no background in filmmaking. The theatrical debut was poorly received, playing only at the Capri Theater in El Paso and some [drive-ins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drive-in "Drive-in") around [West Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Texas "West Texas") and [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico").

*Manos* remained in obscurity until 1993, when it was featured in an episode of *[Mystery Science Theater 3000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystery_Science_Theater_3000 "Mystery Science Theater 3000")*, a television series based around mocking [B movies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B_movie "B movie"), which became the show's most iconic episode. This developed its [cult reputation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_film "Cult film") as one of the [worst films ever made](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_films_considered_the_worst#Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate_\(1966\) "List of films considered the worst").[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) The film has been criticized for continuous deficiencies in editing, continuity, audiovisual synchronization, pacing, acting, and several inexplicable and disconnected scenes, such as a nameless couple repeatedly shown kissing in a distant car and the Master's wives breaking into [catfights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catfight "Catfight").[\[5\]](#cite_note-EW1-5) Its *MST3K* appearance resulted in several DVD releases of the original film and three of the *MST3K* episode.[\[6\]](#cite_note-EW5-6) The original [16 mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16_mm_film "16 mm film") [workprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workprint "Workprint") was discovered in California in 2011, from which a new, remastered version of the film was released on [Blu-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu-ray "Blu-ray") by [Synapse Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synapse_Films "Synapse Films") on October 13, 2015\.[\[7\]](#cite_note-NPR\(2011-12-12\)-7)[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)

The film was followed by a [prequel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prequel "Prequel"), *Manos: The Rise of Torgo* (2018), and a [sequel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequel "Sequel"), *[Manos Returns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manos_Returns "Manos Returns")* (2018).

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

*Manos: The Hands of Fate*, full movie

While on vacation near [El Paso, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Paso,_Texas "El Paso, Texas"), Michael, Margaret, their young daughter Debbie, and their dog, Peppy, drive through the desert in search of the Valley Lodge. Margaret insists they are lost, and Michael claims they are not. They are stopped by a local deputy for a broken taillight, and released because Michael asks him for mercy on their "first vacation". After driving through farmland and the desert, the family reaches a house. The [satyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satyr "Satyr")\-like Torgo is caretaker "while the Master is away". Michael and Margaret ask Torgo for directions to the Valley Lodge, which Torgo denies knowing. Frustrated, Michael asks Torgo to let him and his family stay the night, despite objections from both Torgo and Margaret.

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/The_Master%E2%80%94_Manos_tHoF.jpg/250px-The_Master%E2%80%94_Manos_tHoF.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Master—_Manos_tHoF.jpg)

Painting of the Master (Tom Neyman)

Inside the house, Michael and Margaret find a painting of the Master and a dog with glowing eyes. A howl frightens Margaret; Peppy breaks away from Debbie and runs outside. Michael investigates with a flashlight and [revolver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolver "Revolver") from his car and finds Peppy lying dead on the ground. Michael buries the dog in the desert and returns to the house. Meanwhile, Torgo reveals his attraction to Margaret and wants to keep her, defying the Master's desire to marry her. Margaret threatens to tell Michael of Torgo's advances. However, Torgo convinces Margaret not to say anything by promising to protect her. Michael cannot start the car. Torgo tells them there is no phone in the house, so the family decides to stay the night.

Torgo secretly watches Margaret changing her clothes. Michael and Margaret find Debbie is gone and start looking for her, going outside and shouting Debbie’s name. Debbie returns, holding the leash of the dog from the painting. Following Debbie, Michael and Margaret stumble upon the Master and his wives, sleeping around a blazing fire. The wives are dressed in nightgowns, the Master in a robe with two red hands on it. Margaret and Debbie run back to the house to get their things and escape. As Michael runs behind them, Torgo uses a stick to knock him out and then ties him to a pole. The Master awakens and summons his wives, announcing that Michael must be sacrificed to the [deity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deity "Deity") Manos, and that Margaret and Debbie will become his new wives. He leaves.

The wives argue with each other about whether Debbie should become one of them or also be sacrificed. This turns into a catfight, where the wives tumble around in the dirt. The Master returns, breaks up the fight and decides to sacrifice Torgo and his first wife instead. Meanwhile, Michael wakes up, unties himself and returns to the house to collect Margaret and Debbie. The family runs off into the desert to escape. The Master summons Torgo and hypnotizes him, ordering the wives to kill him. Two of the wives attack Torgo with their hands, causing him to fall to the ground, seemingly dead. However, he later regains consciousness and stands up.

The Master severs and burns Torgo's left hand. Torgo runs off into the darkness with his stump of a wrist in flames, and the Master sacrifices his first wife.

As Michael, Margaret and Debbie run through the desert, Margaret falls and says she cannot go any farther. A [rattlesnake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rattlesnake "Rattlesnake") appears and Michael shoots it, the noise attracting the attention of the deputies, who assume the noises came from Mexico due to the large desert echoes and leave it at that. Margaret convinces Michael to return to the house, as the cult would never think to look for them there. They go back and find the Master and his dog waiting for them. The Master steps towards them, and Michael fires his gun in shock, to no effect.

Some time later, two women starting their vacation drive through a rainstorm, searching for shelter. When they find the Master's house, the entranced Michael greets them, saying "I am Michael, I take care of the place while The Master is away." Margaret and Debbie have become wives of the Master, and all are asleep.

## History

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: History")\]

### Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Production")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/Manos_The_Hands_of_Fate_%281966%29_2.jpg/250px-Manos_The_Hands_of_Fate_%281966%29_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Manos_The_Hands_of_Fate_\(1966\)_2.jpg)

Torgo's [satyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satyr "Satyr")\-like features

Warren was very active in the theater scene in El Paso, Texas, and he once appeared as a [walk-on](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bit_part "Bit part") for the television series *[Route 66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Route_66_\(TV_series\) "Route 66 (TV series)")*, where he met screenwriter [Stirling Silliphant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling_Silliphant "Stirling Silliphant"). While chatting with Silliphant in a local coffee shop, Warren claimed that it was not difficult to make a horror film, and he bet Silliphant that he could make an entire film on his own. After placing the bet, Warren began the first outline of his script on a napkin, right inside the coffee shop.[\[5\]](#cite_note-EW1-5)

Warren financed it with a substantial but insufficient amount of cash, US$19,000 (equivalent to $189,000 in 2025). He hired a group of actors from a local theater, many of whom he had worked with before, and a modeling agency.[\[5\]](#cite_note-EW1-5) Instead of any [wages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wage "Wage"), Warren promised the cast and crew a share of profit.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10)[\[11\]](#cite_note-EW2-11)

In mid-1966, it was filmed with the working titles *The Lodge of Sins* and *Fingers of Fate*. It was shot mainly on the [ranch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranch "Ranch") of Colbert Coldwell, a lawyer who shared an office floor with Warren and who later became a judge in [El Paso County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Paso_County,_Texas "El Paso County, Texas"). Most equipment was rented, so Warren hurriedly maximized the number of shots before the rental deadline. The [16 mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16_mm_film "16 mm film") [Bell & Howell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_&_Howell "Bell & Howell") camera is wound by hand with up to 32 seconds of footage,[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10) creating many unresolved editing problems.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) Rather than using [location sync sound recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sync_sound "Sync sound"), all sound effects and dialogue were [overdubbed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubbing "Dubbing") in post-production by few people, including Warren, Tom Neyman, Reynolds, Jennings, and Warren's wife, Norma.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10)[\[13\]](#cite_note-EW4-13) Later during production, Warren renamed the film *Manos: The Hands of Fate*.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10) Warren's small crew became so bemused by his amateurishness and irascibility that they derisively called the film *Mangos: The Cans of Fruit* behind his back.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10)[\[14\]](#cite_note-YouTube-14)

During filming, Warren said that presenting Diane Mahree as the Texas Beauty Queen would generate good publicity for his movie. He signed her to a regional West Texas [beauty pageant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_pageant "Beauty pageant") that would lead to [Miss Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Texas "Miss Texas") and then to the [Miss America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_America "Miss America") pageant, but he neglected to tell her about it until she was accepted as an entrant. She complied and appeared onstage as a finalist. Warren contracted with a modeling agency to provide the actresses who would play the Master's wives, including Joyce Molleur. She broke her foot early in production, so Warren retained her by rewriting the script to include a young couple kissing in a car on the side of the road, who are otherwise unconnected to the plot.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10)

[![A man and woman kiss in a convertible sports car, with the clapperboard accidentally at the edge of the frame.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/Manos_The_Hands_of_Fate_%281966%29_Clapperboard_Fail.png/250px-Manos_The_Hands_of_Fate_%281966%29_Clapperboard_Fail.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Manos_The_Hands_of_Fate_\(1966\)_Clapperboard_Fail.png)

Editing failed to remove the clapperboard, which is momentarily visible for a few frames.

Warren shot [night-for-night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night-for-night "Night-for-night") scenes, because many of the cast and crew also held day jobs.[\[11\]](#cite_note-EW2-11) In many of the night scenes, the lights attracted swarms of [moths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moth "Moth") in view of the camera. In the scene in which the police investigate Mike's gunfire, the lights could cover only a few feet forward, so the police stood there to feign a search and leave without any scenery or a panning shot.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10)

[Post-production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-production "Post-production") efforts were minimal, though Warren promised crew members that any problems in filming would be fixed in later editing.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10)[\[15\]](#cite_note-interview2-15) For example, the [clapperboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clapperboard "Clapperboard") is momentarily visible.[\[16\]](#cite_note-I-16) The entire nine-minute opening sequence, which consists of the main characters driving around looking for their hotel with minimal dialogue or plot, was the result of such neglect. Warren had likely intended to include [opening credits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opening_credits "Opening credits") over these shots, but either forgot or lacked the post-production budget.[\[17\]](#cite_note-17)

John Reynolds, who played Torgo, committed suicide with a shotgun on October 16, 1966, one month before the premiere.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10) He was 25 years old and this was his only film appearance.[\[18\]](#cite_note-18)

### Release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Release")\]

The film premiered at the Capri Theater in Warren's hometown of [El Paso, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Paso,_Texas "El Paso, Texas") on November 15, 1966, as a benefit for the local [cerebral palsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerebral_palsy "Cerebral palsy") fund.[\[19\]](#cite_note-massaged-19) Warren rented a searchlight[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10) and paid for the cast to be delivered by limousine to enhance the Hollywood feel. The single limousine delivered one group, then drove around the block for another.[\[20\]](#cite_note-EW3-20) Jackey Neyman-Jones, the seven-year-old who played Debbie, wept in disappointment at the premiere, particularly when hearing a woman's dubbed voice instead of her own.[\[21\]](#cite_note-elpasonew-21) Mahree laughed throughout the screening at the film's ridiculousness.[\[22\]](#cite_note-2014interview-22)

Following the premiere, Warren thought *Manos* was the worst film ever made, but was proud of it,[\[6\]](#cite_note-EW5-6) and he suggested that its audio might be re-dubbed into a passable comedy.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10) The film was briefly distributed by Emerson Film Enterprises, with a brief theatrical run at the Capri Theater, and at various [drive-in theaters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drive-in_theater "Drive-in theater") in West Texas and New Mexico, including [Las Cruces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Cruces,_New_Mexico "Las Cruces, New Mexico"). The only compensation was Jackey Neyman's bicycle and her family dog's 50 pounds of [dog food](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dog_food "Dog food").[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10)[\[15\]](#cite_note-interview2-15) Official box office figures are unknown, if they ever existed. Warren won his bet against [Stirling Silliphant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling_Silliphant "Stirling Silliphant"), proving that he was capable of creating an entire film.[\[13\]](#cite_note-EW4-13)

The majority of the cast and crew never appeared in another film, though Mahree had a successful modeling career as Diane Adelson.[\[22\]](#cite_note-2014interview-22) Warren pitched another script he had written called *Wild Desert Bikers*, and then pitched its novelization, but with the failure of *Manos*, there was no interest.[\[6\]](#cite_note-EW5-6)

### Obscurity

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Obscurity")\]

Following few local screenings, *Manos* was almost entirely forgotten. When Jackey Neyman attended the [University of California, Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley "University of California, Berkeley"), her friends could not find a copy of the film.[\[15\]](#cite_note-interview2-15) A 1980 magazine article by cinematographer Bob Guidry's ex-wife Pat Ellis Taylor reports the film may have appeared on a local television station and that it was "listed at the bottom of a page in a film catalogue for rent for $20.00".[\[23\]](#cite_note-23) The film re-surfaced through a 16 mm print, presumably from this television package, which was introduced into the home video collecting market by a number of public domain film suppliers. One of these suppliers was ultimately the one that offered the film to [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central"). It was in a box of films sent to [Frank Conniff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Conniff "Frank Conniff") in 1992, when he chose *Manos* as one of the films to be shown on *[Mystery Science Theater 3000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystery_Science_Theater_3000 "Mystery Science Theater 3000")*.[\[13\]](#cite_note-EW4-13)

## Reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Reception")\]

The day after premiere, Betty Pierce, the film reviewer of the *[El Paso Herald-Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Paso_Herald-Post "El Paso Herald-Post")* described it as a "brave experiment". She criticized some elements, such as the "hero" Torgo being "massaged to death" by the Master's wives and Margaret's claim of "it's getting dark" with a bright midday sun.[\[19\]](#cite_note-massaged-19)

In 2005, Dan Neil of the *[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")* explained the film's appeal: "After screening *Manos* for probably the 10th time, I've concluded it has to do with intimacy. Because it is such a pure slice of Warren's brain – he wrote, directed, produced and starred, and brooked no collaboration – *Manos* amounts to the man's cinematically transfigured subconscious."[\[24\]](#cite_note-LAtimes-24) *Manos* buff Bobby Thompson said, "It's like a train wreck; you just can't take your eyes off it."[\[6\]](#cite_note-EW5-6)

On review aggregator website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), the film has an approval rating of [0%](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_films_with_a_0%25_rating_on_Rotten_Tomatoes "List of films with a 0% rating on Rotten Tomatoes") based on 15 reviews, with an average rating of 2\.56/10.[\[25\]](#cite_note-Rotom-25) The book *Hollywood's Most Wanted* lists *Manos* as the \#2 in the list of "The Worst Movies Ever Made", following *[Plan 9 from Outer Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plan_9_from_Outer_Space "Plan 9 from Outer Space")*.[\[26\]](#cite_note-26) *[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")* proclaimed *Manos* "The Worst Movie Ever Made".[\[5\]](#cite_note-EW1-5) The scene in which the seven-year-old Debbie becomes a wife of the Master, played by her real father, was included in a list of "The Most Disgusting Things We've Ever Seen" by the *Mystery Science Theater 3000* crew.[\[27\]](#cite_note-mst3k-guide-27)

## Legacy

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Legacy")\]

### *Mystery Science Theater 3000* and RiffTrax

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Mystery Science Theater 3000 and RiffTrax")\]

[![A man in giving a presentation to an audience in front of a theatrical curtain](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Frank_Conniff_DragonCon_2008.jpg/250px-Frank_Conniff_DragonCon_2008.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frank_Conniff_DragonCon_2008.jpg)

[Frank Conniff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Conniff "Frank Conniff") chose *Manos* to be featured on *Mystery Science Theater 3000* in 1992\.

On January 30, 1993, the film was featured on the fourth season finale of the [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central") series *[Mystery Science Theater 3000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystery_Science_Theater_3000 "Mystery Science Theater 3000")*, a show about a crew held captive in outer space by two mad scientists, and forced to watch bad movies. *Manos* was far worse than the usual fare, with the long uneventful drive used by the hosts to sarcastically repeat its title numerous times, in lieu of any action to heckle. The host robots eventually sobbed at the film defeating even their attempts at making it interesting, with one of them saying "can you believe this?" at one point. The mad scientists apologized and admitted the film was abysmal beyond their limits for torture. Torgo (played by [Michael J. Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_J._Nelson "Michael J. Nelson")) made a cameo in later episodes.

Selection of *Manos* for the show is credited to [Frank Conniff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Conniff "Frank Conniff"), who also played TV's Frank. Conniff was generally in charge of pre-screening and selecting films sent to them by [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central"), the show's network at the time, and *Manos* was a random tape that he had pulled from a recent batch they had been sent. He felt the movie "seemed like it was maybe a crime against humanity, but you couldn't be sure" and "has an atmosphere, a vibe" that made it appropriate for the show.[\[28\]](#cite_note-playboy-28)[\[29\]](#cite_note-29) The *Manos* episode has been described as one of the best of the *MST3K* series by *[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")*[\[6\]](#cite_note-EW5-6) and *[CraveOnline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CraveOnline "CraveOnline")*,[\[30\]](#cite_note-30) and the *MST3K* episode is credited with bringing to light the otherwise obscure film, even though it led to the film being considered one of the worst films made at user polls at the [Internet Movie Database](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMDb "IMDb").[\[28\]](#cite_note-playboy-28)[\[31\]](#cite_note-31)[\[32\]](#cite_note-32) Kevin Murphy later declared, "I hate this movie. I think I hate this movie more than any other film we ever did at *RiffTrax* or *Mystery Science Theater*. Even more than the [Coleman Francis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coleman_Francis "Coleman Francis") movies. There's something about this movie that just makes my skin crawl."[\[33\]](#cite_note-33) Series creator [Joel Hodgson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_Hodgson "Joel Hodgson"), who hosted the episode, has remained perplexed at its popularity as he felt their riff on the film wasn't great.[\[34\]](#cite_note-34) Following a festival screening of the episode which he attended, Hodgson commented "We have a lot funnier riffs than this."[\[35\]](#cite_note-35) During a Q&A session at the 2008 [San Diego Comic-Con](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_Comic-Con "San Diego Comic-Con"), a question was put to the cast and writers of *MST3K* about any film they passed on that was worse than *Manos*, and many cited the film *[Child Bride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_Bride "Child Bride")*.[\[36\]](#cite_note-36)

*Manos* has also been riffed on by *[RiffTrax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RiffTrax "RiffTrax")*, a later project of *MST3K* alumni Mike Nelson, [Kevin Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Murphy_\(actor\) "Kevin Murphy (actor)") and [Bill Corbett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Corbett "Bill Corbett"), during a live show on August 16, 2012,[\[37\]](#cite_note-37)\[*[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")*\] a live event that was simulcast in film theaters across the United States.[\[38\]](#cite_note-38) While Nelson and Murphy were part of the cast when *MST3K* riffed on *Manos*, neither their fellow RiffTrax star [Bill Corbett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Corbett "Bill Corbett") nor their writers were involved in the original episode; the riffing was all new jokes, using a cleaner print of the original *Manos*, allowing them to joke about things not obvious in the original television episode.[\[39\]](#cite_note-39)

### Cult following

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Cult following")\]

The *MST3K* episode featuring the film was released on [DVD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD "DVD") in 2001, and in the *Mystery Science Theater 3000 Essentials* collection in 2004\.[\[40\]](#cite_note-dvdreview-40)[\[41\]](#cite_note-41)

Four comedy stage adaptations of the film have been made. The first was given in [Portland, Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland,_Oregon "Portland, Oregon") in early 2006\.[\[42\]](#cite_note-New_Production-42) The second, a musical titled *Manos: Rock Opera of Fate*, was launched in October 2007\.[\[43\]](#cite_note-43)\[*[dead link](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Link_rot "Wikipedia:Link rot")*\] The third, a puppet musical titled *Manos – The Hands of Felt*, was performed by Puppet This in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle") in April 2011\.[\[44\]](#cite_note-44) After raising funds with a [Kickstarter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kickstarter "Kickstarter") campaign in May 2013, *Manos – The Hands of Felt* was performed again in Seattle by Vox Fabuli Puppets in August 2013 and filmed for DVD release.[\[45\]](#cite_note-45)[\[46\]](#cite_note-46) The fourth was in [Portland, Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland,_Oregon "Portland, Oregon") in April 2013\.[\[47\]](#cite_note-47)

In March 2015, the murderers on the *[Elementary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elementary_\(TV_series\) "Elementary (TV series)")* episode "[T-Bone And The Iceman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Elementary_episodes#ep65 "List of Elementary episodes")" used the physical features of Torgo (portrayed by John Reynolds) to compose a fake [facial composite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facial_composite "Facial composite") to get the [NYPD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Police_Department "New York City Police Department") off their trail. It worked until they were caught, due to the character of Dr. Joan Watson having recognized Torgo's features from the film. The film's editor, James Sullivan, is the namesake of one of the characters in the episode.[\[48\]](#cite_note-48)

## Restoration

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Restoration")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/Manos%2C_The_Hands_of_Fate_%281966_film%29.jpg/250px-Manos%2C_The_Hands_of_Fate_%281966_film%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Manos,_The_Hands_of_Fate_\(1966_film\).jpg)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Manos_the_Hands_of_Fate_screenshot_from_Solovey_workprint.jpg/250px-Manos_the_Hands_of_Fate_screenshot_from_Solovey_workprint.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Manos_the_Hands_of_Fate_screenshot_from_Solovey_workprint.jpg)

Comparison of the print found in various releases prior to 2015 and the Solovey workprint found in 2011

In 2011, the original [16mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16_mm_film "16 mm film") [workprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workprint "Workprint") of *Manos: The Hands of Fate* was discovered by Ben Solovey, a Florida State film school graduate, in a collection of 16 mm films. Solovey announced his intention to preserve and [restore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_restoration "Film restoration") *Manos* for a [Blu-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu-ray "Blu-ray") release.[\[7\]](#cite_note-NPR\(2011-12-12\)-7)[\[49\]](#cite_note-'Manos'_in_HD-49)[\[50\]](#cite_note-50) His [Kickstarter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kickstarter "Kickstarter") campaign raised $48,000, nearly five times the initial goal. A 90% finished print was premiered at the El Paso [Plaza Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaza_Theatre_\(El_Paso\) "Plaza Theatre (El Paso)"), near the original premiere in 1966\.[\[21\]](#cite_note-elpasonew-21) The new restoration premiered on [Blu-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu-ray "Blu-ray") on October 13, 2015, with an unrestored version ("Grindhouse") as one of the bonus features.[\[51\]](#cite_note-51)

### Copyright dispute

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Copyright dispute")\]

In general, any work first published in the United States before March 1989 required a [copyright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright "Copyright") notice, or the work was not copyrighted.[\[52\]](#cite_note-52) *Manos: The Hands of Fate* is in the [public domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_domain "Public domain") because director Harold Warren failed to include a copyright notice in the film. When news broke of Solovey's restoration, the son of Harold Warren, Joe Warren, started exploring the possibility that the film was not in the public domain, seeking to prevent others from profiting from his father's work. Warren discovered in 2013 that the script had been copyrighted and registered in the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress"), and he believes that this copyright also applies to the film. No [precedent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precedent "Precedent") exists for this case so the legal status of the film is uncertain. Solovey applied copyright on his restored version, an action that Warren believes is unenforceable, though has not sought any legal action against Solovey.[\[28\]](#cite_note-playboy-28) Warren obtained pending publication of a [trademark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trademark "Trademark") on the phrase *Manos: The Hands of Fate*, which could have impacted the various fanworks if the [United States Patent and Trademark Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Patent_and_Trademark_Office "United States Patent and Trademark Office") finalized approval.[\[53\]](#cite_note-53) However, the trademark filing has since been abandoned as of December 6, 2018, for a "failure to respond or late response".[\[54\]](#cite_note-54)

## Home media

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Home media")\]

[Shout Factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shout!_Factory "Shout! Factory") released a [special edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_edition "Special edition") with both the MST3K and uncut versions called *Manos y Manos*. A DVD of the original was published by [Alpha Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Video "Alpha Video"),[\[55\]](#cite_note-Aplha-55) which also released original versions of other MST3K films such as *[Teenagers from Outer Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teenagers_from_Outer_Space_\(film\) "Teenagers from Outer Space (film)")* and *[Eegah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eegah "Eegah")*.[\[56\]](#cite_note-TeenAlpha-56)

## Sequels

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Sequels")\]

### *Manos: The Search for Valley Lodge*

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Manos: The Search for Valley Lodge")\]

In 2010, writer and director Rupert Talbot Munch, Sr. began work on *Manos: The Search for Valley Lodge*. Tom Neyman (in a cameo reprising his role as the Master), his daughter Jackey Neyman-Jones (reprising her role as Debbie), Diane Mahree (reprising the role of Margaret), and Bernie Rosenblum (who played a teenage boy in the original film) were involved in initial filming. Others engaged to appear included [World Wrestling Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wrestling_Entertainment "World Wrestling Entertainment") star [Gene Snitsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Snitsky "Gene Snitsky"), former WWE diva and Playboy centerfold [Maria Kanellis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Kanellis "Maria Kanellis"), and UFC fighter [Ryan "Big Deal" Jimmo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Jimmo "Ryan Jimmo"). Munch was to play Torgo.[\[57\]](#cite_note-57)

In 2013, Neyman-Jones left the project after disagreements with Munch,[\[58\]](#cite_note-58) and by the end of 2014, the project was reportedly canceled.[\[59\]](#cite_note-59)

### *Manos: The Rise of Torgo*

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Manos: The Rise of Torgo")\]

In 2013, a project began for a prequel titled *Manos: The Rise of Torgo*. David Roy (producer of the 2014 film *Cheeseballs*) was announced as the writer and director, and cast members were to include Neyman-Jones (playing Manos, the evil deity).[\[60\]](#cite_note-60)[\[61\]](#cite_note-61) It was released on Amazon Prime streaming in 2018\.[\[62\]](#cite_note-62)\[*[non-primary source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No_original_research#Primary,_secondary_and_tertiary_sources "Wikipedia:No original research")*\]

### *Manos Returns*

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Manos Returns")\]

Main article: [Manos Returns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manos_Returns "Manos Returns")

Jackey Neyman-Jones, who played Debbie in the original film, launched a Kickstarter campaign in February 2016 to make a sequel titled *Manos Returns*. According to Neyman-Jones, the sequel was not to be a recreation of *Manos* but instead a "tongue-in-cheek" setting within the *Manos* storyline; Neyman-Jones described the planned product as being both funny and scary, similar to *[The Cabin in the Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cabin_in_the_Woods "The Cabin in the Woods")* or *[Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbott_and_Costello_Meet_Frankenstein "Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein")*.[\[63\]](#cite_note-63)[\[64\]](#cite_note-64)[\[65\]](#cite_note-65)

The Kickstarter goal of $24,000 was reached on February 24, 2016\. It stars Neyman-Jones, reprising her role as Debbie; her father Tom Neyman, reprising his role as the Master; and Diane Mahree reprising her role as Margaret. Neyman-Jones and director Tonjia Atomic shot the film in western Oregon in the summer of 2016\. The film had its world premiere screening at Crypticon Seattle on May 4, 2018\.[\[66\]](#cite_note-66) *Manos Returns* was published on [Amazon Prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Prime "Amazon Prime") in May 2020\.[\[67\]](#cite_note-67)

### *The Manos Chronicles*

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: The Manos Chronicles")\]

A 4-episodes TV series titled *The Manos Chronicles* has been distributed in 2023 on Amazon Prime. It stars Jackey Neyman reprising her role as Debbie.

## Video game

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Video game")\]

Main article: [Manos: The Hands of Fate (video game)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate_\(video_game\) "Manos: The Hands of Fate (video game)")

A video game based on the film for [iOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOS "IOS") was released in 2012 by FreakZone Games. A [Microsoft Windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") port and an [Android](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Android_\(operating_system\) "Android (operating system)") port were later released.[\[68\]](#cite_note-IGN-68)

***Manos: The Hands of Fate*** is a 1966 [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") [independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_film "Independent film") [folk horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_horror "Folk horror") film written, directed, and produced by Harold P. Warren.[\[3\]](#cite_note-AFIsearch-3) It stars Warren, Tom Neyman, John Reynolds, and Diane Mahree. It was released on November 15, 1966\. The film follows a family getting lost during their vacation road trip through the [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas") desert and becoming stranded at the lodge of a [polygynous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygyny "Polygyny") [pagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pagan "Pagan") [cult](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult "Cult") led by the Master who decides their fate.

Warren was an [insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurance "Insurance") and fertilizer salesman from [El Paso, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Paso,_Texas "El Paso, Texas"), who made the film as a result of a bet with screenwriter [Stirling Silliphant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling_Silliphant "Stirling Silliphant"). Most of the remaining cast and crew had little or no background in filmmaking. The theatrical debut was poorly received, playing only at the Capri Theater in El Paso and some [drive-ins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drive-in "Drive-in") around [West Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Texas "West Texas") and [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico").

*Manos* remained in obscurity until 1993, when it was featured in an episode of *[Mystery Science Theater 3000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystery_Science_Theater_3000 "Mystery Science Theater 3000")*, a television series based around mocking [B movies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B_movie "B movie"), which became the show's most iconic episode. This developed its [cult reputation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_film "Cult film") as one of the [worst films ever made](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_films_considered_the_worst#Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate_\(1966\) "List of films considered the worst").[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) The film has been criticized for continuous deficiencies in editing, continuity, audiovisual synchronization, pacing, acting, and several inexplicable and disconnected scenes, such as a nameless couple repeatedly shown kissing in a distant car and the Master's wives breaking into [catfights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catfight "Catfight").[\[5\]](#cite_note-EW1-5) Its *MST3K* appearance resulted in several DVD releases of the original film and three of the *MST3K* episode.[\[6\]](#cite_note-EW5-6) The original [16 mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16_mm_film "16 mm film") [workprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workprint "Workprint") was discovered in California in 2011, from which a new, remastered version of the film was released on [Blu-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu-ray "Blu-ray") by [Synapse Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synapse_Films "Synapse Films") on October 13, 2015\.[\[7\]](#cite_note-NPR\(2011-12-12\)-7)[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)

The film was followed by a [prequel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prequel "Prequel"), *Manos: The Rise of Torgo* (2018), and a [sequel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequel "Sequel"), *[Manos Returns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manos_Returns "Manos Returns")* (2018).

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

*Manos: The Hands of Fate*, full movie

While on vacation near [El Paso, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Paso,_Texas "El Paso, Texas"), Michael, Margaret, their young daughter Debbie, and their dog, Peppy, drive through the desert in search of the Valley Lodge. Margaret insists they are lost, and Michael claims they are not. They are stopped by a local deputy for a broken taillight, and released because Michael asks him for mercy on their "first vacation". After driving through farmland and the desert, the family reaches a house. The [satyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satyr "Satyr")\-like Torgo is caretaker "while the Master is away". Michael and Margaret ask Torgo for directions to the Valley Lodge, which Torgo denies knowing. Frustrated, Michael asks Torgo to let him and his family stay the night, despite objections from both Torgo and Margaret.

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/The_Master%E2%80%94_Manos_tHoF.jpg/250px-The_Master%E2%80%94_Manos_tHoF.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Master—_Manos_tHoF.jpg)

Painting of the Master (Tom Neyman)

Inside the house, Michael and Margaret find a painting of the Master and a dog with glowing eyes. A howl frightens Margaret; Peppy breaks away from Debbie and runs outside. Michael investigates with a flashlight and [revolver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolver "Revolver") from his car and finds Peppy lying dead on the ground. Michael buries the dog in the desert and returns to the house. Meanwhile, Torgo reveals his attraction to Margaret and wants to keep her, defying the Master's desire to marry her. Margaret threatens to tell Michael of Torgo's advances. However, Torgo convinces Margaret not to say anything by promising to protect her. Michael cannot start the car. Torgo tells them there is no phone in the house, so the family decides to stay the night.

Torgo secretly watches Margaret changing her clothes. Michael and Margaret find Debbie is gone and start looking for her, going outside and shouting Debbie’s name. Debbie returns, holding the leash of the dog from the painting. Following Debbie, Michael and Margaret stumble upon the Master and his wives, sleeping around a blazing fire. The wives are dressed in nightgowns, the Master in a robe with two red hands on it. Margaret and Debbie run back to the house to get their things and escape. As Michael runs behind them, Torgo uses a stick to knock him out and then ties him to a pole. The Master awakens and summons his wives, announcing that Michael must be sacrificed to the [deity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deity "Deity") Manos, and that Margaret and Debbie will become his new wives. He leaves.

The wives argue with each other about whether Debbie should become one of them or also be sacrificed. This turns into a catfight, where the wives tumble around in the dirt. The Master returns, breaks up the fight and decides to sacrifice Torgo and his first wife instead. Meanwhile, Michael wakes up, unties himself and returns to the house to collect Margaret and Debbie. The family runs off into the desert to escape. The Master summons Torgo and hypnotizes him, ordering the wives to kill him. Two of the wives attack Torgo with their hands, causing him to fall to the ground, seemingly dead. However, he later regains consciousness and stands up.

The Master severs and burns Torgo's left hand. Torgo runs off into the darkness with his stump of a wrist in flames, and the Master sacrifices his first wife.

As Michael, Margaret and Debbie run through the desert, Margaret falls and says she cannot go any farther. A [rattlesnake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rattlesnake "Rattlesnake") appears and Michael shoots it, the noise attracting the attention of the deputies, who assume the noises came from Mexico due to the large desert echoes and leave it at that. Margaret convinces Michael to return to the house, as the cult would never think to look for them there. They go back and find the Master and his dog waiting for them. The Master steps towards them, and Michael fires his gun in shock, to no effect.

Some time later, two women starting their vacation drive through a rainstorm, searching for shelter. When they find the Master's house, the entranced Michael greets them, saying "I am Michael, I take care of the place while The Master is away." Margaret and Debbie have become wives of the Master, and all are asleep.

## History

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: History")\]

### Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Production")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/Manos_The_Hands_of_Fate_%281966%29_2.jpg/250px-Manos_The_Hands_of_Fate_%281966%29_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Manos_The_Hands_of_Fate_\(1966\)_2.jpg)

Torgo's [satyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satyr "Satyr")\-like features

Warren was very active in the theater scene in El Paso, Texas, and he once appeared as a [walk-on](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bit_part "Bit part") for the television series *[Route 66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Route_66_\(TV_series\) "Route 66 (TV series)")*, where he met screenwriter [Stirling Silliphant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling_Silliphant "Stirling Silliphant"). While chatting with Silliphant in a local coffee shop, Warren claimed that it was not difficult to make a horror film, and he bet Silliphant that he could make an entire film on his own. After placing the bet, Warren began the first outline of his script on a napkin, right inside the coffee shop.[\[5\]](#cite_note-EW1-5)

Warren financed it with a substantial but insufficient amount of cash, US$19,000 (equivalent to $189,000 in 2025). He hired a group of actors from a local theater, many of whom he had worked with before, and a modeling agency.[\[5\]](#cite_note-EW1-5) Instead of any [wages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wage "Wage"), Warren promised the cast and crew a share of profit.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10)[\[11\]](#cite_note-EW2-11)

In mid-1966, it was filmed with the working titles *The Lodge of Sins* and *Fingers of Fate*. It was shot mainly on the [ranch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranch "Ranch") of Colbert Coldwell, a lawyer who shared an office floor with Warren and who later became a judge in [El Paso County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Paso_County,_Texas "El Paso County, Texas"). Most equipment was rented, so Warren hurriedly maximized the number of shots before the rental deadline. The [16 mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16_mm_film "16 mm film") [Bell & Howell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_&_Howell "Bell & Howell") camera is wound by hand with up to 32 seconds of footage,[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10) creating many unresolved editing problems.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) Rather than using [location sync sound recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sync_sound "Sync sound"), all sound effects and dialogue were [overdubbed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubbing "Dubbing") in post-production by few people, including Warren, Tom Neyman, Reynolds, Jennings, and Warren's wife, Norma.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10)[\[13\]](#cite_note-EW4-13) Later during production, Warren renamed the film *Manos: The Hands of Fate*.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10) Warren's small crew became so bemused by his amateurishness and irascibility that they derisively called the film *Mangos: The Cans of Fruit* behind his back.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10)[\[14\]](#cite_note-YouTube-14)

During filming, Warren said that presenting Diane Mahree as the Texas Beauty Queen would generate good publicity for his movie. He signed her to a regional West Texas [beauty pageant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_pageant "Beauty pageant") that would lead to [Miss Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Texas "Miss Texas") and then to the [Miss America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_America "Miss America") pageant, but he neglected to tell her about it until she was accepted as an entrant. She complied and appeared onstage as a finalist. Warren contracted with a modeling agency to provide the actresses who would play the Master's wives, including Joyce Molleur. She broke her foot early in production, so Warren retained her by rewriting the script to include a young couple kissing in a car on the side of the road, who are otherwise unconnected to the plot.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10)

[![A man and woman kiss in a convertible sports car, with the clapperboard accidentally at the edge of the frame.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/Manos_The_Hands_of_Fate_%281966%29_Clapperboard_Fail.png/250px-Manos_The_Hands_of_Fate_%281966%29_Clapperboard_Fail.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Manos_The_Hands_of_Fate_\(1966\)_Clapperboard_Fail.png)

Editing failed to remove the clapperboard, which is momentarily visible for a few frames.

Warren shot [night-for-night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night-for-night "Night-for-night") scenes, because many of the cast and crew also held day jobs.[\[11\]](#cite_note-EW2-11) In many of the night scenes, the lights attracted swarms of [moths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moth "Moth") in view of the camera. In the scene in which the police investigate Mike's gunfire, the lights could cover only a few feet forward, so the police stood there to feign a search and leave without any scenery or a panning shot.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10)

[Post-production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-production "Post-production") efforts were minimal, though Warren promised crew members that any problems in filming would be fixed in later editing.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10)[\[15\]](#cite_note-interview2-15) For example, the [clapperboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clapperboard "Clapperboard") is momentarily visible.[\[16\]](#cite_note-I-16) The entire nine-minute opening sequence, which consists of the main characters driving around looking for their hotel with minimal dialogue or plot, was the result of such neglect. Warren had likely intended to include [opening credits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opening_credits "Opening credits") over these shots, but either forgot or lacked the post-production budget.[\[17\]](#cite_note-17)

John Reynolds, who played Torgo, committed suicide with a shotgun on October 16, 1966, one month before the premiere.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10) He was 25 years old and this was his only film appearance.[\[18\]](#cite_note-18)

### Release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Release")\]

The film premiered at the Capri Theater in Warren's hometown of [El Paso, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Paso,_Texas "El Paso, Texas") on November 15, 1966, as a benefit for the local [cerebral palsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerebral_palsy "Cerebral palsy") fund.[\[19\]](#cite_note-massaged-19) Warren rented a searchlight[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10) and paid for the cast to be delivered by limousine to enhance the Hollywood feel. The single limousine delivered one group, then drove around the block for another.[\[20\]](#cite_note-EW3-20) Jackey Neyman-Jones, the seven-year-old who played Debbie, wept in disappointment at the premiere, particularly when hearing a woman's dubbed voice instead of her own.[\[21\]](#cite_note-elpasonew-21) Mahree laughed throughout the screening at the film's ridiculousness.[\[22\]](#cite_note-2014interview-22)

Following the premiere, Warren thought *Manos* was the worst film ever made, but was proud of it,[\[6\]](#cite_note-EW5-6) and he suggested that its audio might be re-dubbed into a passable comedy.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10) The film was briefly distributed by Emerson Film Enterprises, with a brief theatrical run at the Capri Theater, and at various [drive-in theaters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drive-in_theater "Drive-in theater") in West Texas and New Mexico, including [Las Cruces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Cruces,_New_Mexico "Las Cruces, New Mexico"). The only compensation was Jackey Neyman's bicycle and her family dog's 50 pounds of [dog food](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dog_food "Dog food").[\[10\]](#cite_note-Interview-10)[\[15\]](#cite_note-interview2-15) Official box office figures are unknown, if they ever existed. Warren won his bet against [Stirling Silliphant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling_Silliphant "Stirling Silliphant"), proving that he was capable of creating an entire film.[\[13\]](#cite_note-EW4-13)

The majority of the cast and crew never appeared in another film, though Mahree had a successful modeling career as Diane Adelson.[\[22\]](#cite_note-2014interview-22) Warren pitched another script he had written called *Wild Desert Bikers*, and then pitched its novelization, but with the failure of *Manos*, there was no interest.[\[6\]](#cite_note-EW5-6)

### Obscurity

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Obscurity")\]

Following few local screenings, *Manos* was almost entirely forgotten. When Jackey Neyman attended the [University of California, Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley "University of California, Berkeley"), her friends could not find a copy of the film.[\[15\]](#cite_note-interview2-15) A 1980 magazine article by cinematographer Bob Guidry's ex-wife Pat Ellis Taylor reports the film may have appeared on a local television station and that it was "listed at the bottom of a page in a film catalogue for rent for $20.00".[\[23\]](#cite_note-23) The film re-surfaced through a 16 mm print, presumably from this television package, which was introduced into the home video collecting market by a number of public domain film suppliers. One of these suppliers was ultimately the one that offered the film to [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central"). It was in a box of films sent to [Frank Conniff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Conniff "Frank Conniff") in 1992, when he chose *Manos* as one of the films to be shown on *[Mystery Science Theater 3000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystery_Science_Theater_3000 "Mystery Science Theater 3000")*.[\[13\]](#cite_note-EW4-13)

## Reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Reception")\]

The day after premiere, Betty Pierce, the film reviewer of the *[El Paso Herald-Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Paso_Herald-Post "El Paso Herald-Post")* described it as a "brave experiment". She criticized some elements, such as the "hero" Torgo being "massaged to death" by the Master's wives and Margaret's claim of "it's getting dark" with a bright midday sun.[\[19\]](#cite_note-massaged-19)

In 2005, Dan Neil of the *[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")* explained the film's appeal: "After screening *Manos* for probably the 10th time, I've concluded it has to do with intimacy. Because it is such a pure slice of Warren's brain – he wrote, directed, produced and starred, and brooked no collaboration – *Manos* amounts to the man's cinematically transfigured subconscious."[\[24\]](#cite_note-LAtimes-24) *Manos* buff Bobby Thompson said, "It's like a train wreck; you just can't take your eyes off it."[\[6\]](#cite_note-EW5-6)

On review aggregator website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), the film has an approval rating of [0%](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_films_with_a_0%25_rating_on_Rotten_Tomatoes "List of films with a 0% rating on Rotten Tomatoes") based on 15 reviews, with an average rating of 2\.56/10.[\[25\]](#cite_note-Rotom-25) The book *Hollywood's Most Wanted* lists *Manos* as the \#2 in the list of "The Worst Movies Ever Made", following *[Plan 9 from Outer Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plan_9_from_Outer_Space "Plan 9 from Outer Space")*.[\[26\]](#cite_note-26) *[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")* proclaimed *Manos* "The Worst Movie Ever Made".[\[5\]](#cite_note-EW1-5) The scene in which the seven-year-old Debbie becomes a wife of the Master, played by her real father, was included in a list of "The Most Disgusting Things We've Ever Seen" by the *Mystery Science Theater 3000* crew.[\[27\]](#cite_note-mst3k-guide-27)

## Legacy

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Legacy")\]

### *Mystery Science Theater 3000* and RiffTrax

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Mystery Science Theater 3000 and RiffTrax")\]

[![A man in giving a presentation to an audience in front of a theatrical curtain](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Frank_Conniff_DragonCon_2008.jpg/250px-Frank_Conniff_DragonCon_2008.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frank_Conniff_DragonCon_2008.jpg)

[Frank Conniff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Conniff "Frank Conniff") chose *Manos* to be featured on *Mystery Science Theater 3000* in 1992\.

On January 30, 1993, the film was featured on the fourth season finale of the [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central") series *[Mystery Science Theater 3000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystery_Science_Theater_3000 "Mystery Science Theater 3000")*, a show about a crew held captive in outer space by two mad scientists, and forced to watch bad movies. *Manos* was far worse than the usual fare, with the long uneventful drive used by the hosts to sarcastically repeat its title numerous times, in lieu of any action to heckle. The host robots eventually sobbed at the film defeating even their attempts at making it interesting, with one of them saying "can you believe this?" at one point. The mad scientists apologized and admitted the film was abysmal beyond their limits for torture. Torgo (played by [Michael J. Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_J._Nelson "Michael J. Nelson")) made a cameo in later episodes.

Selection of *Manos* for the show is credited to [Frank Conniff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Conniff "Frank Conniff"), who also played TV's Frank. Conniff was generally in charge of pre-screening and selecting films sent to them by [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central"), the show's network at the time, and *Manos* was a random tape that he had pulled from a recent batch they had been sent. He felt the movie "seemed like it was maybe a crime against humanity, but you couldn't be sure" and "has an atmosphere, a vibe" that made it appropriate for the show.[\[28\]](#cite_note-playboy-28)[\[29\]](#cite_note-29) The *Manos* episode has been described as one of the best of the *MST3K* series by *[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")*[\[6\]](#cite_note-EW5-6) and *[CraveOnline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CraveOnline "CraveOnline")*,[\[30\]](#cite_note-30) and the *MST3K* episode is credited with bringing to light the otherwise obscure film, even though it led to the film being considered one of the worst films made at user polls at the [Internet Movie Database](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMDb "IMDb").[\[28\]](#cite_note-playboy-28)[\[31\]](#cite_note-31)[\[32\]](#cite_note-32) Kevin Murphy later declared, "I hate this movie. I think I hate this movie more than any other film we ever did at *RiffTrax* or *Mystery Science Theater*. Even more than the [Coleman Francis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coleman_Francis "Coleman Francis") movies. There's something about this movie that just makes my skin crawl."[\[33\]](#cite_note-33) Series creator [Joel Hodgson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_Hodgson "Joel Hodgson"), who hosted the episode, has remained perplexed at its popularity as he felt their riff on the film wasn't great.[\[34\]](#cite_note-34) Following a festival screening of the episode which he attended, Hodgson commented "We have a lot funnier riffs than this."[\[35\]](#cite_note-35) During a Q&A session at the 2008 [San Diego Comic-Con](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_Comic-Con "San Diego Comic-Con"), a question was put to the cast and writers of *MST3K* about any film they passed on that was worse than *Manos*, and many cited the film *[Child Bride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_Bride "Child Bride")*.[\[36\]](#cite_note-36)

*Manos* has also been riffed on by *[RiffTrax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RiffTrax "RiffTrax")*, a later project of *MST3K* alumni Mike Nelson, [Kevin Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Murphy_\(actor\) "Kevin Murphy (actor)") and [Bill Corbett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Corbett "Bill Corbett"), during a live show on August 16, 2012,[\[37\]](#cite_note-37)\[*[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")*\] a live event that was simulcast in film theaters across the United States.[\[38\]](#cite_note-38) While Nelson and Murphy were part of the cast when *MST3K* riffed on *Manos*, neither their fellow RiffTrax star [Bill Corbett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Corbett "Bill Corbett") nor their writers were involved in the original episode; the riffing was all new jokes, using a cleaner print of the original *Manos*, allowing them to joke about things not obvious in the original television episode.[\[39\]](#cite_note-39)

### Cult following

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Cult following")\]

The *MST3K* episode featuring the film was released on [DVD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD "DVD") in 2001, and in the *Mystery Science Theater 3000 Essentials* collection in 2004\.[\[40\]](#cite_note-dvdreview-40)[\[41\]](#cite_note-41)

Four comedy stage adaptations of the film have been made. The first was given in [Portland, Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland,_Oregon "Portland, Oregon") in early 2006\.[\[42\]](#cite_note-New_Production-42) The second, a musical titled *Manos: Rock Opera of Fate*, was launched in October 2007\.[\[43\]](#cite_note-43)\[*[dead link](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Link_rot "Wikipedia:Link rot")*\] The third, a puppet musical titled *Manos – The Hands of Felt*, was performed by Puppet This in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle") in April 2011\.[\[44\]](#cite_note-44) After raising funds with a [Kickstarter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kickstarter "Kickstarter") campaign in May 2013, *Manos – The Hands of Felt* was performed again in Seattle by Vox Fabuli Puppets in August 2013 and filmed for DVD release.[\[45\]](#cite_note-45)[\[46\]](#cite_note-46) The fourth was in [Portland, Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland,_Oregon "Portland, Oregon") in April 2013\.[\[47\]](#cite_note-47)

### Copyright dispute

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Manos:_The_Hands_of_Fate&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Copyright dispute")\]

In general, any work first published in the United States before March 1989 required a [copyright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright "Copyright") notice, or the work was not copyrighted.[\[52\]](#cite_note-52) *Manos: The Hands of Fate* is in the [public domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_domain "Public domain") because director Harold Warren failed to include a copyright notice in the film. When news broke of Solovey's restoration, the son of Harold Warren, Joe Warren, started exploring the possibility that the film was not in the public domain, seeking to prevent others from profiting from his father's work. Warren discovered in 2013 that the script had been copyrighted and registered in the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress"), and he believes that this copyright also applies to the film. No [precedent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precedent "Precedent") exists for this case so the legal status of the film is uncertain. Solovey applied copyright on his restored version, an action that Warren believes is unenforceable, though has not sought any legal action against Solovey.[\[28\]](#cite_note-playboy-28) Warren obtained pending publication of a [trademark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trademark "Trademark") on the phrase *Manos: The Hands of Fate*, which could have impacted the various fanworks if the [United States Patent and Trademark Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Patent_and_Trademark_Office "United States Patent and Trademark Office") finalized approval.[\[53\]](#cite_note-53) However, the trademark filing has since been abandoned as of December 6, 2018, for a "failure to respond or late response".[\[54\]](#cite_note-54)

**Analysis summary:**

The barcode's statistical fingerprint is highly distinctive:

- **~17% pitch-black stripes** and ~37% near-dark overall, with long continuous black runs (one ~5% of runtime, and the whole final quarter mostly dark)
- **Washed-out, muddy palette** — mean saturation only 0.25, virtually zero vivid stripes (1.4%), dominated by warm sepia/tan/olive earth tones
- **Pale, gray-green/blue "daylight" opening** covering roughly the first 13–19% (mean luminance 85, desaturated — like faded desert daylight)
- Warm rust-brown interior sections mid-film, olive-green outdoor sections, and a very dark ending with deep forest-green stripes

This matches *Manos: The Hands of Fate* almost perfectly:

1. **The famous nine-minute opening** of the family driving through the Texas desert in daylight = the pale, washed-out first ~13% of the barcode (9 min / 70 min runtime)
2. **Night-for-night shooting with grossly underexposed lighting** (lights only reached a few feet, moths swarming the camera) = the enormous near-black stretches, especially the pitch-black runs
3. **Shot on 16mm Ektachrome reversal** with faded, muddy color = the consistently low-saturation sepia/olive look — no vivid primaries anywhere
4. Texas desert scrub (tan/olive), the lodge's warm brown/rust interior and fireplace glow = the middle sections
5. Runtime 70 min → each 1px stripe ≈ 4.2 seconds, i.e. "a few seconds" per stripe
6. The stormy, dark finale (two women driving in a rainstorm, night at the lodge) = the dark ending stripes

The alternatives all fail the profile: *Day of the Dead* would be teal/blue-gray; *American Werewolf in Paris* and *Wish Upon* are glossy saturated modern looks; *Prom Night* has vivid colored disco lighting in its final act; *Black Christmas* has reds/blues of decorations and cool night exteriors; *The Messengers* is full of bright gold sunflower fields; *Nosferatu* has rich blues/ochres; *Sleepaway Camp* is a bright, saturated summer-camp film with far less darkness.

**Answer: G**
